claims.text: A nanolaminate spinel oxide coating on CoCrFeNi will form and stabilize a lubricious protective sliding interface.
The coating will suppress friction and wear throughout approximately 25–800 °C.
Uncoated CoCrFeNi has acceptable sliding performance only at moderate temperatures and develops increased friction and accelerated wear at elevated temperatures.
The elevated-temperature deterioration of uncoated CoCrFeNi is caused by oxidation and unstable surface phases.
The proposed nanolaminate spinel oxide coating is thermally stable over the test regime.
The intervention produces a retained, self-adaptive, low-shear spinel oxide layer at the sliding interface.
At low temperatures, the coating acts as a robust and adherent barrier.
Increasing temperature causes controlled coating oxidation and an in-situ transition to a dense, lubricious spinel structure.
The spinel structure minimizes contact between the CoCrFeNi substrate and the counterface.
Reduced substrate–counterface contact lowers friction and wear.
The coated material will have lower coefficient of friction and wear rate than uncoated CoCrFeNi over the entire temperature span.
The largest performance improvements will occur near 800 °C.
Testing is bounded to an ambient oxidizing environment and temperatures from approximately 25 °C to 800 °C.
Prior reports show improved high-temperature behavior from in-situ spinel oxides in related systems.
Long-term coating adhesion, phase stability, and self-renewal across the full temperature range remain uncertain.
Failure to obtain a statistically significant reduction in both friction coefficient and wear rate over the entire range relative to uncoated controls will falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The intervention is described as an already-spinel oxide coating, whereas the mechanism says oxidation induces an in-situ transition of that coating to a spinel structure; the precursor and resulting phase are therefore not consistently distinguished.
The conditions describe continuously increasing temperature, while the experimental design specifies incrementally raising temperature.
